en: "By this confession, I confess; knowing and remembering, I do not conceal it"—this is the confession of misdeeds.
Then, having placed his right knee upon the ground and having placed a flower in the hand of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he should thus entreat three times:
"O spiritual friend, grant me refuge in the Three Jewels.
Thereupon, the spiritual friend should say with a resolute intention (adhyāśaya): "I grant it."
Then, for the purpose of taking refuge in the Three Jewels, one should have him recite the formal motion (*jñapti*).
The recitation of the scriptural formula for the sake of the vow (*saṃvara*), performed in the sequence of prostrations, kneeling, and joining the palms, is called the *jñapti*.
In this regard, the *jñapti* is as follows:

Pay heed, Venerable One! I, [name], from this moment until the end of my life, go for refuge to the Buddha, the Blessed One—the Great Compassionate One, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing, who has transcended all enmity, the Great Being with an indestructible body, the Unsurpassed Body, the Dharma Body, the foremost among two-legged beings.
Pay heed, Venerable Sir! I, [name], from this moment until the end of my life, go for refuge to the Dharma, the peaceful, the supreme among those free from passion.
Again, pay attention, Venerable Sir: I, named so-and-so, from this moment until the end of my life, go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the best of assemblies.
One should cause each person to recite it three times.
Then the teacher should speak what is appropriate, and the disciple should say "Excellent! regarding taking refuge in the Three Jewels.

This, however, is the refuge in general for the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, both in their conventional and ultimate senses. Therein, the conventional Buddha consists of the [relic] element, stūpas, images, caityas, and so forth; the ultimate Buddha is that which has the three bodies (trikāya) as its essence.
The conventional dharma is the teaching (*pravacana*), while its ultimate meaning is the absolute (*pāramārthika*).

The conventional Saṅgha consists of laymen (*upāsaka*), laywomen (*upāsikā*), monks (*bhikṣu*), nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), and Bodhisattvas; however, the ultimate Saṅgha consists of the Noble Ones (*ārya*). Among them, the laymen include Bimbisāra and others; the laywomen include Viśākhā and others; the monks include Maudgalyāyana and others; the nuns include Gautamī and others; and the Bodhisattvas include the Noble Maitreya and others.

All of these are indeed worthy of refuge; however, there is this distinction: noble ones may exist even while remaining in the householder stage of life (*gṛhāśrama*). They are not to be saluted even by non-noble ascetics (*yatibhiḥ*). Furthermore, if noble ones are junior in their vows (*vratakaniṣṭha*), they too are not to be saluted by those who are senior in their vows (*vratajyeṣṭha*). Thus it is said in the *Vinaya*: "In the Saṅgha there are those who have entered the path of practice (*pratipannaka*), but there are none who have fully realized the proper conduct (*sāmīcīpratipannaka*); there are those who possess both," and so forth. This, however, has been explained in detail in the *Abhidharma*.
And this has not been written here for fear of excessive prolixity.

One who takes refuge in this very Three Jewels is called a "Buddhist. This refuge in the other three jewels is the seed for all the vows (*saṃvara*) of the Buddhist system, beginning with those of the lay follower (*upāsaka*). Regarding those vows, how many in number are they? They are enumerated in the *Vibhāṣā*: there are eight, beginning with the lay follower and ending with the *poṣadha* (fasting) observance. In the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna, there are exactly those same eight previously mentioned, with the addition of the ninth, the bodhisattva vow (*bodhisattvasaṃvara*).

In the Mahāyāna of the Mantra system, there are exactly those previously mentioned nine, with the *vajravratasamvara* as the tenth. Among them, there are seven vows based on the distinction between male and female supports for the seven classes: the layman (*upāsaka*), the laywoman (*upāsikā*), the novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), the monk (*bhikṣu*), the novice nun (*śrāmaṇerī*), the trainee nun (*śikṣamāṇā*), and the nun (*bhikṣuṇī*). Apart from these, there is no distinction among the *poṣadha* vows and so forth. Accordingly, a monk who has become such for that day is to be saluted by both the nun and the novice who have long practiced their vows; such indeed is the established order of the vows.
Furthermore, in that regard, the laymen (*upāsaka*), laywomen (*upāsikā*), and bodhisattvas who have undertaken the *poṣadha* vows should be addressed.
Now, the daily practice of Buddhists is described as consisting merely in taking refuge in the Three Jewels.
Since the ultimate Buddha is unattainable, the conventional Buddha alone is to be honored as the Teacher. And so says the scripture:

"Whoever honors, reveres, respects, and venerates the Tathāgata while he is still present, or who, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, shall fashion even an image the size of a barley grain and honor it—of these two, an equal ripening of the fruit is to be expected. There is no distinction or difference between them," and so forth.
Furthermore,
there is no distinction in merit between one who honors [the Buddha] while he is still present and one who honors him after he has passed into parinirvāṇa, provided their clarity of mind is equal.

The Dharma should always be meditated upon; it is to be honored specifically in the form of a book. However, the worship of the Dharma in its ultimate sense is indeed the worship of the Buddha and the Saṅgha.

And the Saṅgha should be accepted as the Teacher himself, being the incomparable object of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*) through gifts of robes, alms-food, bedding, seats, medicines, and so forth; and one should maintain the perception of the Buddha while honoring the Saṅgha. This very practice of taking refuge in the Three Jewels and so on, when performed with wealth through white karma, will unfailingly grant rebirth in a happy state. And thus says the scripture:
The ripening of exclusively white actions is exclusively white; that of black actions is black; and that of mixed actions is mixed.

The ripening of these [karmas] through their differentiation is to be understood from the *Karmapluti* and other sūtras; and because of that [ripening], it is also [to be understood] from the treatises on the six destinies (*ṣaḍgati*) and so forth.
In this context, black karma consists of the killing of living beings and so forth, because its maturation is black. To illustrate this, a mere indication is shown here:
"Those men who are killers of humans through five factors go to the Saṃjīva hell, having increased [the suffering] of sentient beings or having slain them."
Having killed goats, sheep, jackals, rabbits, rats, deer, pigs,
and other living beings, they will certainly go to the Saṃghāta hell.
Those who speak slander and untruth go to the Kālasūtra hell.
They go to the Raurava hell, as do others who steal dogs.
17cd.
The adulterer is made to climb by force against his will the Śālmalī tree, which has sixteen-finger-long thorns with sharp, glowing iron tips, while he cries out in agony.
Intoxication arises from the drinking of liquor; it produces a lack of discernment, and through it, evils are brought forth. Thus, one should avoid liquor.

This very class of actions, such as the killing of living beings, performed through an unrighteous livelihood or for the sake of sensual gratification, when being committed, is called non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). And it comes to reside in the left side of the belly.

Due to their association with that [lack of restraint], fishermen, hunters, fowlers, and the like, as well as eunuchs, by their very nature are not fit for restraint; for these individuals, restraint should not be granted.
Furthermore, according to the tradition (āgama), when fishermen and others abandon their livelihood through acts such as taking life, then restraint may be granted to them.

Specifically, even among black actions, the mere abstention from them constitutes white action; and when practiced as an unimpaired and unassailed state, it becomes virtue (*śīla*) and that which is wholesome beyond measure.
For this very reason, it is said that the ten wholesome [actions] arise precisely from the avoidance of the ten unwholesome ones.

If this very same wholesome action is undertaken through a formal declaration (*jñapti*) and then abandoned by the virtuous, then in their bodies, the white karma residing in the right side arises in the form of the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and so forth.

Without even making a formal vow, those who do not commit evil obtain a mere merit that lacks continuity; however, this white karma in the form of restraint (*saṃvara*)—because it is the cause for the uninterrupted accumulation of merit even during states of non-distraction or mindlessness, and because it brings about the attainment of the celestial realms such as Tuṣita—is of great fruit. Therefore, its procedure is now described.
In that regard, furthermore, this is the procedure for [initiating someone as] a lay follower (*upāsaka*).

Having had him perform the worship of the Buddha and so forth, up to taking refuge in the Three Jewels, according to the previously mentioned sequence, there is the formal announcement (*jñapti*) of the five precepts (*śikṣāpada*) in their entirety.
Or, depending on his incapacity, having had him recite the announcement even in a partial manner, one should make him a lay follower.
In this regard, the formal motion (*jñapti*) is as follows:

"Pay attention, Venerable One! Just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, have abstained from the taking of life; even so, I, [name], from this day forward for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, shall abstain from the taking of life. By this first limb, I train myself in the training of those noble Arhats, I conform to it, and I imitate it.
This is to be repeated three times.

Pay heed, Venerable Sir: just as those noble Arhats have for as long as life lasts abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, and have abstained from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants; [so may you do].

"In this way, I, [name], from this day forward for as long as life lasts, having abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, I abstain from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants. By means of this fifth limb, I shall train in, conform to, and follow the training of those noble Arhats. This should be recited three times. Then the teacher should say, "It is proper," and the student should say, "So be it."
Thus, one is a lay follower (*upāsaka*) by means of these five trainings (*śikṣā*). And likewise, there is this statement addressed to the lay follower Naktaṅka:

"One should not take life, nor should one take what belongs to another; one should not, even in thought, approach the wife of another; one should not speak falsehood, nor drink *vāruṇī* liquor; one should train oneself in these five points here."

But he who, by accepting [the Buddha] as Teacher and so forth, takes refuge in the Three Jewels and practices even a portion of the training, is a *prādeśika* (partial) lay follower (*upāsaka*); such is the procedure for undertaking the vows of a lay follower.

Now, the vow of a bodhisattva has a greater fruit than all other vows. Thus it is said: "Throughout the succession of aeons, while practicing the conduct of awakening, the Buddhas have seen that the single vow known as that of a bodhisattva alone is beneficial."
Through faith in this, the one who grasps it shall become worthy of veneration by the three worlds;
liberated from all evil, he is proclaimed a son of the Buddha.
From the moment he first resolves his mind with an irreversible intention upon the liberation of the boundless realm of sentient beings, [he becomes a bodhisattva].
From that time forward, even while he is asleep or heedless,
uninterrupted streams of merit flow forth repeatedly, as vast as the sky.
Furthermore,
an iron wheel twelve yojanas in diameter revolves above his head.
It is said in scripture that [the fault] has been removed through the generation of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).
If the merit arising from the vow of the thought of awakening were to have form,
it would fill the entire realm of space and even exceed it.
Thus, having heard of the preeminent fruit of the bodhisattva vow, those who seek the state of Buddhahood must certainly pursue it, even amidst the honors of the three realms.
This concludes the ritual procedure for the bodhisattva vow.
Here too, having drawn the three maṇḍalas and completed everything as before, one should go for refuge to the Three Jewels.
However, the distinction here is that in place of the phrase "for as long as life lasts," one says "until sitting at the seat of enlightenment.

Then, immediately after taking refuge in the Three Jewels, a layman or laywoman, or a male or female renunciant who wishes to receive the bodhisattva vows, should honor [the preceptor] with great reverence. Having received the vows, the preceptor should be requested with these responses. This is the request:

"O son of good family, I desire to receive from you the undertaking of the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline (*bodhisattvasamvaraśīla*). Therefore, out of compassion for me, it would be fitting for you to grant and listen to this for a moment.

Having placed a flower in the hands of the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one should recite this three times: "I shall favor him with the undertaking of the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline from my presence. When the spiritual friend has recited this three times, the disciple must respond, "I accept."

Immediately thereafter, having caused the student to arrange the upper robe over one shoulder, he should perform a respectful salutation (*sāmīcī*) toward the infinite Buddhas existing in the ten directions and the three times with a boundless clarity of mind.
Furthermore, the qualities of the Buddhas should be brought within the scope of the student’s intellect;
however, at this juncture, the following quality [is to be emphasized].
Through the attainment of the middle way, he does not abide in nirvana;
therefore, he abides in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) by virtue of attaining the purity of suchness (tathatā).
"Since the Buddha possesses such qualities, for that very reason he stands upon the ground of the Splendor of Qualities (*guṇaśrī*), which is to be looked up to by all embodied beings.

Having thus performed everything, one should again entreat [the teacher] three times, saying: "O spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), please grant me the undertaking of the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline (*bodhisattvaśīlasamvara*)."

Having established one-pointed mindfulness and further increasing clarity of mind, the disciple should remain silent while reflecting on this very purpose: "Before long, I shall now attain the inexhaustible, immeasurable, and unsurpassed great treasure of merit. Then, whether the teacher is standing or seated, the disciple should ask him as follows: "Listen, O you of such-and-such name, are you a Bodhisattva who has made the vow for awakening? The disciple should respond three times with "Oṃ," having thus made his formal declaration. Three times.

Then, the teacher should speak again as follows: "Do you, [Name], wish to receive from me all the bodhisattva training rules and the entire bodhisattva ethical discipline—that ethical discipline which was included among the bodhisattvas of the past, and those training rules and that ethical discipline which will belong to the bodhisattvas of the future?"

One should say three times: "I accept those training rules and that ethical discipline which belong to the bodhisattvas currently existing in the ten directions, and those training rules in which the bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present have trained and are training."

Then, having caused the disciple to generate the bodhisattva vow, one should have him recite this: "Pay heed, Venerable Sir! I, [name], for the sake of crossing over the infinite realm of sentient beings, for their upliftment, for their protection from the sufferings of saṃsāra, and for establishing them in the unsurpassed knowledge of the omniscient one—"

Just as the bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, having generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), have attained, are attaining, and will attain Buddhahood; just as all Buddhas know and see with unobstructed Buddha-knowledge and the Buddha-eye; and just as, having known the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, they grant their approval—by that same method, I, [name], in the presence of the preceptor and before all Buddhas and bodhisattvas, generate the mind for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
"I generate the mind for perfect enlightenment for the sake of the awakening of embodied beings;
I shall practice the conduct of excellence that brings about the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having recited this three times, the teacher should say: "It is well; the disciple has performed what was appropriate."
Thus concludes the procedure for undertaking the bodhisattva vows.
Immediately thereafter, the undertaking of the ethical discipline (*śīla-samādāna*) must be formally promised through a threefold ritual action;
for that purpose, this is the procedure:

"May all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas assembled from the world-systems of the ten directions attend to me! May the Preceptor attend to me! I, named so-and-so, dedicate this root of merit produced by the vow of the Bodhisattva ethical discipline toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

In this world that is without protection, without refuge, without shelter, without a final resort, and without an island, may I become a protection, a refuge, a guide, a final resort, and an island. And may I ferry across all sentient beings who have not yet crossed over from the cycle of existence; may I lead those who have not attained final nirvāṇa to final nirvāṇa through the various practices of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); may I provide rest for those without rest and give hope to those without hope—thus, three times.
Thus is the undertaking of ethical discipline.

Therefore, may all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas assembled from the world-systems of the ten directions attend to me; may the Preceptor attend to me. I, who am named [so-and-so], having generated the thought of enlightenment, regard the infinite realm of sentient beings as my mother, father, sister, brother, son, daughter, or any other relative or kinsman.

In this way I accept; and having accepted, I apply the roots of virtue according to my capacity, according to my strength, and according to what is appropriate—whatever gift I shall give, whatever morality I shall maintain, whatever patience I shall perfect, whatever vigor I shall undertake, whatever meditative concentration I shall attain, whatever wisdom I shall investigate, and whatever skill in means I shall train in.

"For the sake, the happiness, and the welfare of all sentient beings, and for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, I follow the conduct of the Great Vehicle of those compassionate Bodhisattvas who are established on the great stages; I train in this, thinking, 'I am a Bodhisattva, by these [precepts],' and from this moment forth, may you hold me as your teacher. Thus he says three times, until: "As long as the first limit of cyclic existence, which is devoid of end, lasts, for so long shall I practice the immeasurable conduct for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings."
I generate the mind set on perfect enlightenment in the presence of the Protector;
I invite the entire world, and thus I shall liberate them from poverty.
From this day forward, until I attain enlightenment, I shall never harbor a mind defiled by malice, nor envy, nor stinginess.
I shall practice the holy life; I shall abandon evil desires.
I will train myself in emulation of the Buddhas in the restraint and discipline of ethical conduct.
I do not intend to attain awakening in a hurried manner;
for the sake of even a single sentient being, I shall remain until the furthest limit of the future.
I shall purify a field that is immeasurable and inconceivable;
and I shall establish a name renowned in all directions.
I shall purify bodily and vocal actions in every respect;
I shall purify mental action; as the doer of deeds, I shall perform nothing unwholesome.
The teacher should perform what is appropriate, and the disciple should respond, "Very well."

Then, that preceptor, having prostrated at the feet of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwelling, remaining, and staying in the ten directions before that image, and having performed the proper salutation, should announce as follows:

"I have thus received from the Bodhisattva named [so-and-so] the undertaking of the Bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline in the presence of the Bodhisattva named [so-and-so], even up to three times. Therefore, I, named [so-and-so], acknowledge myself as having that Bodhisattva named [so-and-so] as my witness. I announce this to the Bodhisattva named [so-and-so], and furthermore to the supreme Noble Ones who are beyond perception, to all sentient beings everywhere, and to the Buddhas who perceive even what is imperceptible throughout the infinite and boundless world-systems in the ten directions."

In this undertaking of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline, it is in three ways; and furthermore, immediately after the taking up of the vow of ethical discipline, it is indeed the nature of things that in the infinite and boundless world-systems of the ten directions, a sign appears to the Tathāgatas who are staying, remaining, and maintaining themselves, as well as to the bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages, by which they come to know: "The attainment of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline has been received by a bodhisattva of such-and-such a name from a bodhisattva of such-and-such a name."
The procedure for undertaking [the precepts] from another has been explained.

Because this bodhisattva vow is like a golden vessel, it can be reassembled even after being broken. Regarding its restoration—whether for the first time or upon subsequent repair—they state that there is a procedure for receiving the vow from images and the like in the total absence of a guru. In that regard, the procedure is as follows:

The disciple must recite this; indeed, the disciple must recite what has been taught by the Guru, with the resolute intention that "it is being recited by the Buddhas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions. Thus, following the aforementioned sequence, the disciple must perform everything along with its constituent parts.
This is the formal declaration of the Bodhisattva vow.

Now, even for one remaining in the householder stage of life (*gṛhāśrama*), because celibacy (*brahmacarya*) yields great fruit, one should practice celibacy according to the sequence of the *poṣadha*. And that [celibacy] may be practiced for as long as life lasts through a formal commitment; or for a day and night due to its incomparable nature; or for a day alone or a night alone; or by one who has gone for refuge to the Three Jewels; or by a lay follower (*upāsaka*).

"I shall practice the holy life (brahmacarya)," [he thinks], due to the vow of the Bodhisattvas. Or rather, for a Bodhisattva, if there should be a desire among those who abide in other philosophical systems (darśanāntara), then, according to the statement in the *Abhidharma*, he should practice the holy life by means of taking refuge in the Three Jewels—whose protection is uninterrupted during the time of the Poṣadha—through the eight precepts (śikṣāpada). Furthermore, in the Āgama, it is said that this has three names: Poṣadha, Upoṣadha, and Upavāsa.
And likewise, having recollected birth, sickness, old age, and death, as if experiencing them himself:
Especially on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the full moon day.
Having taken refuge in the Three Jewels for even a single day and night, the wise person should always diligently observe the eightfold *upoṣadha* vow.

Here too, as before, having caused the three mandalas and the worship of the Buddhas and so forth to be performed, one should cause [the disciple] to take refuge in the Three Jewels. Then, for the sake of the *poṣadha*, after having the disciple—who has been requested [to receive it]—recite the *poṣadha* motion (*jñapti*), one should cause him to take the *poṣadha* vow. In this regard, the motion is as follows:

Pay heed, venerable sir: just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, have abstained from the taking of life—having laid aside the rod, having laid aside the weapon, being modest and compassionate toward all beings, including even the smallest insects such as ants; so too, I, [name], from this moment until the coming night, [shall likewise abstain].

And until tomorrow at sunrise, in the interval between now and then, having abandoned the taking of life, I shall abstain from the taking of life. By this first limb, I, [name], train myself in the training of those noble Arhats; I conform to it; I imitate it. Thus three times.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, attend to this: just as those noble Arhats have abandoned taking what is not given, unchaste conduct, false speech, and the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants for as long as life lasts; and having abandoned dancing, singing, instrumental music, wearing garlands, perfumes, ointments, ornaments, and cosmetics, as well as high beds, large beds, and eating at improper times—they have abstained from eating at improper times.

Thus, I, [name], from this moment until the coming night and until tomorrow’s sunrise, in the interval between these times, having abandoned taking what is not given, unchaste conduct, false speech, the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, dancing, singing, music, the wearing of garlands, perfumes, ointments, ornaments, and cosmetics, high beds, large beds, and eating at improper times—I abstain from eating at improper times.

By this eighth factor, I, [name], train in the training of those noble Arhats; I conform to it and imitate it. Thus three times have I bestowed upon myself this Poṣadha, the undertaking of the restraint of ethical discipline, for the adornment of the mind, for the equipment of the mind, for the attainment of the unsurpassed fruit.
The teacher should speak what is appropriate, and the disciple should say, "Excellent."
Thus ends the formal proclamation for the poṣadha as spoken in the *Poṣadhānuśaṃsa-sūtra*.

Furthermore, this Poṣadha restraint is not granted to male novices (śrāmaṇera), female novices (śrāmaṇerī), monks (bhikṣu), or nuns (bhikṣuṇī) on the basis of a lifelong commitment, because for them the Poṣadha is obligatory throughout their lives. It is established that it is granted to others [only] for a limited duration. Specifically, the popular saying "one who has taken the Poṣadha for life" refers only to the Poṣadha itself; however, there is no scriptural authority (āgama) for such a thing. Such a person enters into the status of a male or female novice. [The question arises: "What is the use of the householder's life? This concludes the procedure for undertaking the Poṣadha.

A householder who has undertaken the vows of an upāsaka or the vows of a bodhisattva should train in the ten paths of action consisting of the abstention from unwholesome deeds; one who has undertaken the poṣadha should perform the formal ritual of the poṣadha.
In that regard, the ten unwholesome paths of action are to be understood according to their division into body, speech, and mind:
killing, as well as taking what is not given and sexual misconduct— these three are based on the body and consist of five factors each.
False speech, harshness, and frivolous chatter— these,
together with slander, are said to be the fourfold fault of speech.
Covetousness is the longing for sense objects; ill-will is the thought of malice;
and taking hold of the view that "nothing exists"—these are considered the threefold mental [unwholesome actions].
It is traditionally taught that there are ten unwholesome [paths of action] for those who are born;
because they serve as the basis for these faults, they are recited right here.

In that regard, when one kills a living being with the perception that it is a living being and with a murderous intent—either killing it oneself or causing others to kill it by means of signals and so forth—this constitutes a fundamental offense (*maulāpatti*) through the killing of a human. By this, there is a loss of the vow (*saṃvara*). Thus, for one who kills a human, there is a fundamental offense [only] when the five factors are present, and not otherwise;
for the killing of other sentient beings, even with the five factors, it is merely a misdeed (*duṣkṛta*).
For one who kills a human being when the five factors are absent, there is great misdeed; however, if it is through a mental disposition, it is a mental [misdeed].
It is exactly thus, and not otherwise, regarding living beings—[19r–19v missing].
The desire for what is improper (*viṣamaspṛhā*) is the wish that, by some means, one might appropriate the property and other possessions of others.
Ill-will is hatred toward sentient beings; it is a state of mind such as "May they be killed," "May they be beaten," and so forth.

False view consists of such [assertions] as: "There is no other world, there is no fruit of karma, and there are no gods, Buddhas, or Blessed Ones," and so forth. Furthermore, there is the progressive intensification of malicious speech and the other [non-virtues], namely: causing a schism in the Saṅgha; violating noble ones; violating one's gurus or teachers; obstructing those engaged in the Dharma; having improper longing for the gains and honors of one's gurus or teachers; and the performance of an act of immediate retribution—this is false view.
These ten unwholesome paths of action, born of greed, delusion, and hatred, are inherently reprehensible and are the causes for rebirth in miserable states such as the hells.
This ripening fruit for those who practice the ten unwholesome paths of action has been indicated in the *Ārya-saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-mahāyāna-sūtra*.
Furthermore, it is stated specifically in the *Karmaphala-nirdeśa-sūtra*:

"O monks, by practicing, cultivating, and frequently performing all ten unwholesome paths of action to an excessive degree, one is reborn in the hells; by practicing them to a middling degree, one is reborn among animals; and by practicing them to a mild degree, one is reborn among the hungry ghosts. Such is their ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) and their outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*). It is also stated elsewhere in that very same [sūtra]:

It is explained [or stated]: upon the exhaustion of karma, having emerged from the ripening of hellish states and attained the commonality of human beings, they experience the outflowing fruit (*niḥsyanda-phala*). Through killing, they are of little vitality and short life; through taking what is not given, they suffer the loss of wealth and have bodies that are discolored and soiled; through malicious speech, they are like stones and their friends are divided; through harsh speech, they are angry, possess unpleasant voices, are divisive, and rely on evil.

Through frivolous speech, one’s words become untrustworthy and one’s digestion becomes irregular; through covetousness, one possesses subtle fruits and intense passion; through malice, one is exceedingly hateful and one’s virtues are harsh; through wrong view, one possesses intense delusion and one’s actions become fruitless.
Thus, [this] is the outflow fruit within the human state.

Now, regarding these ten unwholesome actions, it is evident that the loss of the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and others occurs through the root unwholesome deeds. One might wonder: is this loss of vows for them irreversible, like the loss of vows for monks and nuns, or is it reversible? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "In the case of the loss of one's own vow, there is indeed the re-taking of the vow; for even in the case of a lay follower whose vow has been lost, the *Bhikṣuvinaya* states that the granting of the vows of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) and so forth may again take place, preceded by the taking of the lay follower's vow."

According to the Āgama, these ten unwholesome paths of action reach exhaustion through the power of the basis (*āśrayabala*), through confession (*deśanā*), and also through the thorough knowledge of reality (*tattvaparijñāna*). They reach exhaustion completely and without remainder. However, according to the *Bhikṣuvinaya*, a root offense (*maulāpatti*) committed by monks does not reach exhaustion until it has given its maturation (*vipāka*) and its outflow (*nisyanda*).
With this intention, it is stated in that very same [text]:
For indeed, actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the proper time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.
It is said that for this very reason, it is observed that for those dwelling in the householder's stage of life, all transgressions go to destruction through confession.

And likewise, in the *Śūkarikā-avadāna*, a certain son of the gods subject to death was reborn in the womb of a sow in a pit; seeing through the power of knowledge bound to birth that his karma—destined to be experienced and ready to yield its fruit—was imminent, he became agitated in mind and informed Śakra. Upon merely performing the going for refuge as caused by Śakra, he eradicated all that transgression, and having passed away from the Trāyastriṃśa gods, was reborn among the Tuṣita gods.
Furthermore, it is heard in the Āgama that for those such as Aṅgulimāla and Ajātaśatru, all transgressions were indeed exhausted;

this is also stated in the *Caturdharmaka-mahāyāna-sūtra* regarding even the monks: "Mental misdeeds and transgressions, even fundamental (mūlāpatti) ones, go to exhaustion through confession by one whose mind is distressed, thinking, 'What have I done?
And so it is said:
Even after committing most dreadful sins, they become diminished through self-reproach;
by means of confessing them and undertaking restraint, I declare their complete uprooting from the very foundation.
Having committed even a small evil, the ignorant man sinks downward; having committed even a great [evil], the wise man abandons all misfortunes.
For even a small piece of iron sinks in water when it is compacted.
Even that which is great floats when it has been made into a vessel.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Dṛḍhāśaya-mahājñāna-sūtra* and other such scriptures for the sake of the destruction of evil:

"For those who have directly realized suchness (*tathatā*), no accumulation of even committed evils is ever found; nor do they commit further evils—how, then, could they be bound by them? It is with this very intention that it is said.
Although both the auspicious and the inauspicious are devoid of intrinsic nature,
one should nevertheless perform only what is auspicious and not what is inauspicious,
within the conventional reality of the world that resembles the reflection of the moon in water.
Happiness is pleasant, while suffering is perpetually unpleasant.

Those who do not practice even with their minds these ten paths of unwholesome action are called "practitioners of the ten wholesome actions. Furthermore, as stated in the *Karmaphalanirdeśasūtra*, the ten wholesome paths of action, characterized by the abstention from the ten unwholesome ones, are the foundation for birth among gods and humans; they are the basis for the attainment of the fruits of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); and they are the foundation for the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, for the noble [path] regarding all sentient beings, and indeed for all the qualities of a Buddha.

Furthermore, in the *Ārya-Jayamati-paripṛcchā*, it is stated in detail that those who seek the excellence of gods and humans should undertake the ten paths of virtuous action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*).
For this very reason, in the *Vinaya*, the non-commission of evil is called "purity" (*śaucya*) because it is the cause of supreme purification.
And so it is said:
The Fully Awakened Ones have proclaimed that internal purity for the sake of ultimate purification consists in the non-committing of evil through body, mind, and speech.
Purity that is free from the smearing of perfumes is the purification of the mind;
for people who commit evil deeds, what is the use of water or even clay?

Thus, according to the Abhidharma and Vinaya, the ten paths of unwholesome action have been explained along with their swift results. As for those trainings which are specific to Bodhisattvas, they should be studied in works such as the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*. || @ ||

For Buddhists who have gone for refuge to the Three Jewels, whatever training has been taught by the Blessed One in the *Vinaya* and other scriptures regarding the morning duties—beginning with the elimination of feces and urine—is here stated in general terms. Thus one should act; having acted, [one should perform] the task of voiding excrement and urine at dawn.
Thereafter, one should likewise wash the anus with water and earth.
Then, for the sake of purification, seven applications of earth are prescribed for the left hand;
likewise, seven are prescribed separately for each of both hands.
Thus, one should diligently wash the hands and other limbs with abundant water;
otherwise, Śāriputra, this [practice] would be rendered foul-smelling.

Thereafter, if one wishes to consecrate water and a tooth-stick for the purpose of cleansing the mouth, one should consecrate them in this manner: "Oṃ jambhe mohe hṛdayam āvartani hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having recited this twenty-one times, one should consecrate the water. It serves as fruit for his food and the pleasure of eating.

Oṃ, homage to the Three Jewels; homage to Hārītī, the great yakṣiṇī; for food and drink, haḥ, svāhā! With this [mantra], one should consecrate the tooth-stick and the water; then, with that consecrated water and tooth-stick, one should perform the rinsing of the mouth and the use of the tooth-stick.

Bathing has also been taught by the Blessed One: having consecrated water with the mantra *oṃ sarvāṅgakutsitapūtiṃkara hūṃ*, one should bathe oneself while visualizing oneself in that very form through direct bathing, using this mantra.
In this regard, the mantra is as follows:
"Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon their birth..."
In that manner, I shall bathe you with pure, divine water.
Oṃ, to the glory of the samaya of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas, hūṃ hūṃ!

If one is unable to perform a bath by immersion in water—even after having performed the washing of hands and feet and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) without a mantra—one should nevertheless perform the "mantra-bath" using this very mantra. This mantra is also to be used for the bathing of an image.

Then, having performed the washing of hands and feet and the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) with the mantra *oṃ hrīḥ svāhā*, one should pay homage to the Three Jewels and to the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Great Compassionate One. Having consecrated [the water] twenty-one times with this mantra, *tadyathā oṃ akace vikace svāhā*, and having put on the lower garment and upper robe, one should empower the sesame seeds with *oṃ āḥ vajratila hūṃ* and empower the *kuśa* grass with *oṃ āḥ vajradarbha hūṃ*.

Then, with this mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate puṣpaketurājāya tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya tadyathā oṃ puṣpe puṣpe mahāpuṣpe supuṣpe puṣpodbhave puṣpasaṃbhave puṣpāvakīrṇe svāhā*, one should consecrate a flower seven times. By means of a single flower, the fruit of ten million flowers shall be obtained.

Then, if one wishes to perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should recite: *Oṃ āḥ, to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas headed by Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, Śākyamuni, and Maitreya—Vajrāmṛtodake hūṃ svāhā.*

Having consecrated the sesame seeds (*tila*), one should offer handfuls of water together with flowers and *kuśa* grass as desired. [The mantra is: *Oṃ āḥ pitṛbhyo vajrāmṛtodake hūṃ svāhā*. In this same way, for the sake of supreme merit, one should offer to the mother and others, and likewise to the deceased (*preta*s). When offering water to the father and others, the specific difference is that one uses *kuśāṇyaṇa* [grass].

If one should wish to perform the twilight ritual (*sandhyā*), then, having visualized Vajravārāhī—the deity of the twilight ritual—from the *Abhidhānottarottaratantrarāja*, according to the sequence of our disciple’s practice; or, in her absence, having visualized the mantra, the twilight ritual should be performed by one authorized in the special method on a riverbank or another suitable place for meditation.
The fruit of this deity and of the Gāyatrī has been taught in detail in the Abhidhānottara-tantra and the Herukābhyudaya-tantra; therefore, effort should also be made here [in this regard].

If one wishes to offer water to Jambhala, then one should place an image of Maṇibhadra-Jambhala in a vessel made of copper or other materials; or else, having meditated upon Jambhala as the transformation of the seed-syllable *jaṃ*, one should visualize him seated with his feet treading upon the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma. (Or:
"In front [of him are] the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, whose faces are turned toward [him].")
He wears a crown of Vajrasūrya and a yellow lotus garland;
with his two hands, he holds a mongoose and a citron.
Seated upon a moon-disc throne cultivated by the syllable *ka*,
together with the fluids of the eternal [deities] and others arising from the five seed-syllables beginning with *vaṃ*.
One should offer water mixed with [rice], without extending the index finger, having consecrated it with the mantra:
*oṃ jambhalajalendrāya svāhā*.
Then one should offer unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) as a fruit-oblation together with the *bali* offering mixed with the three sweets,
and perform worship with flowers, incense, and so forth, according to one's ability.

Homage to the Three Jewels! Homage to Māṇibhadra, the great commander of the yakṣa army! Oṃ jambhalajalendrāya svāhā! One should also recite this one hundred and eight times, and offer handfuls of water before him. With this very mantra, or with the previously mentioned mantra, one should present the bali-offering, food offerings, and so forth. If anyone should wish to construct a caitya or to strike a sacrificial cake (saccaka), the procedure for that purpose is now stated.

In this regard: Homage to the Triple Gem! Homage to Vairocana-prabhurāja, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha! It is thus: Oṃ, subtle one, subtle one; at the moment, at the moment; peaceful one, tamed one; in the placement, in the supportless; in the crossing over; O Yaśovatī, of great splendor; O Rāhula, in Nirvāṇa, empowered by the empowerment of all Buddhas, svāhā!
Having recited this dhāraṇī twenty-one times over a lump of sand or a lump of clay, one should fashion a caitya.

What, then, is the fruit of this? He said: "As many atoms as there are in that [lump], so many tens of millions of caityas are thereby made. One obtains as much merit as is the number of those atoms and becomes a lord of the ten stages (*daśabhūmīśvara*). And swiftly, one shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vairocana: "Great indeed is the benefit of this dhāraṇī."

Then, having established [the foundation] with this verse: "Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, and also their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa," one should worship with flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth. Then, reciting this very dhāraṇī: *Oṃ namo bhagavate ratnaketurājāya tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya tadyathā oṃ tneramai mahāratne ratnavijaye svāhā*, one should perform the veneration of the caitya.

Thus, by means of a single prostration to a caitya, a prostration to ten million caityas is accomplished. Oṃ, in the pure intrinsic nature, bring forth, bring forth; come, come, O you who are the womb of the *dharmadhātu*, svāhā! This is the dismissal.
Oṃ ākāśadharmadhātugarbhe svāhā. [This is] the confession of faults (*kṣamāpanam*).

Alternatively, according to the opinion of the Saṃmatīyas: having established [the deity] with the mantra "The cause for the granting of the boon of the gift of merit" (*deyadharmavaradahetu*), and having performed the worship and so forth, the dismissal is performed with the mantra "Name-and-form is impermanent" (*nāmarūpam anityam*).
Now, the ritual for the actual striking is explained according to the *Mahāmaṇḍalavyūha Tantra*:
Homage to all Buddhas! To the one with the vajra weapon, svāhā!
With either of these two, one should take up the clay, reciting: *oṃ vajrodbhavāya svāhā*.
The mantra for moving the image.
Oṃ, O stainless one, O free from stain, svāhā!
The mantra for anointing with oil.
Oṃ vajradhātugarbhe svāhā.
The mantra for casting the mudrā.
Oṃ vajramudgare ākoṭaya oṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
The mantra for striking:
Oṃ vajrakartari cchedaya oṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
The mantra for cutting away excess clay.
Oṃ dharmarate svāhā.
The mantra for summoning with a mudrā.
Oṃ, to the one with a well-established face, svāhā!
The mantra for installation.
Oṃ, you who are brilliantly illuminated by the jewels of all the Tathāgatas, blaze, blaze within the womb of the Dharmadhātu! Svāhā!
The consecration mantra.
Having worshipped with flowers, incense, and so forth according to one's ability, one should perform a salutation:
*oṃ svabhāvaśuddhe āhara āhara āgaccha dharmadhātugarbhe svāhā*.
The dismissal: Oṃ ākāśadharmadhātugarbhe svāhā.
The mantra for seeking forgiveness.
One should install the shrine and other such items in a location that has not been damaged.
The benefits of these two have already been stated; how much more [benefit] is now being described? And so it is said in the *Prasenajitparipṛcchā*:

"Endowed with natural beauty and excellent qualities, their senses guarded, and possessing a radiance like the sun, those who cause an image of the Jina to be made here become a delight to the eyes of the world."
The body of that person becomes stainless, liberated from disease, sorrow, and the suffering of existence—
just like the noble youth Padmagarbha— who fashions the body of the Sugata.

Those who have an image of the Jina fashioned here do not go into servitude, nor into a state of poverty, nor into the condition of being a messenger, nor even into a low birth; nor do they suffer any deficiency of the sense faculties.

One who has received the vows beginning with the going for refuge to the Three Jewels must certainly worship the Buddha, the Blessed One, by means of unbroken observance of those commitments. This is the procedure for that:

having performed the consecration of the flowers and water with the previously mentioned mantras, one should wash the hands and feet, and put on the lower garment and upper robe. With the mantra "Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should sprinkle them with the flower-water and perform the protection of the ground for the duration of the observance.

Having empowered flowers, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken rice with the mantra: "Oṃ maṇidhāri vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa 2 māṃ hūṃ svāhā," and having placed them upon one's head for the sake of protection and auspiciousness, one should empower the seat with "Oṃ hūṃ.
Then, by performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the head, throat, and heart with "Oṃ āḥ hūṃ," one effects the empowerment of body, speech, and mind.

Reciting "Oṃ, drive away all obstacles, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should take fragrant substances such as sandalwood and sprinkle them upon the site of the maṇḍala. Then, with the mantra "Oṃ aṇvacadri bhūme hūṃ," one should perform the ritual appropriation of the ground (*bhūmiparigraha*). With the mantra "Oṃ aṇvacadri rekhe hūṃ," one should draw the excellent lines of the maṇḍala. Thereafter, while sweeping the maṇḍala, one should recite this verse on the benefits of the maṇḍala: "Charity is cow dung mixed with water; ethical discipline is the sweeping."
Patience is the removal of minor sores; vigor is the arousal of activity;
meditation is the making of the mind one-pointed for that moment; and wisdom is the brilliant, well-drawn lines—these very six perfections one obtains by having constructed the maṇḍala of the Sage.
He becomes golden-hued, liberated from all diseases, distinguished among gods and men, with a radiant splendor like the moon;
he is born into a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold.
"O Ānanda, having performed bodily actions in this most excellent abode of the Sugata, which is so richly endowed?"
Then, taking a single flower with the left hand,

one should place it upon the back of the right hand while reciting "Oṃ surekhe sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭheta svāhā," and while having it offered in the center of the maṇḍala, one should consecrate its base by resolving it into the form of the moon and sun while reciting "Oṃ candrārkavimale svāhā."

Following that, according to the instruction "one should worship the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas residing in the sky after having drawn them forth," one should emanate the previously arranged three syllables—*tri-akṣara*, *treśa*, and *rīnagāmana*—and with those rays of light, by uttering the syllable *jaṃ*, draw from the region of the sky the Perfectly Enlightened One surrounded by the eight Bodhisattvas. Having caused him to enter that maṇḍala with the syllable *hūṃ*, having bound him with the syllable *vaṃ*, and having gratified him with the syllable *hoḥ*, one should visualize him in his proper place.

In the center there, the Blessed One sits upon a lion throne marked with a vajra, in the vajraparyaṅka posture, possessing a golden hue; his left hand is placed palm-upward in his lap, while his right hand—adorned with the light of a saffron robe and a ushnisha upon his head—is raised in the gesture of granting protection.

In the east is yellow-colored Lokeśvara, wearing a crown of matted hair, holding a white lotus in his left hand. In the south is yellow-colored Maitreya, wearing a crown of matted hair, holding in his left hand a nāga-keśara sprout together with a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). In the west is green Gaganagañja, wearing a jewel crown, holding in his left hand a white lotus joined with a jewel-vase. In the north is yellow-colored Samantabhadra, wearing a jewel crown, holding in his left hand a jewel-tuft (ratnacūḍā).

In the southeast is Vajrapāṇi, green in color, wearing a jewel crown, and holding a blue utpala lotus in his left hand. In the southwest is yellow-colored Mañjuśrī, wearing a jewel crown and holding a blue utpala lotus and a Prajñāpāramitā manuscript in his left hand. In the northwest is Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, green in color, wearing a jewel crown, and holding a green sword and a white lotus in his left hand.

In the northeast is Kṣitigarbha, fair-complexioned, wearing a jewel crown, holding in his left hand a white lotus adorned with a yellow eight-spoked wheel; all these [deities] have their right hands in the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*), are seated upon lotus-moon seats, and sit in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*). Having thus meditated, one should offer everything together with water contained in a conch or other vessel, along with flowers, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), using the mantra: *oṃ jaḥ vaṃ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ khaṃ raṃ*. Likewise, in due order, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the feet using the mantra: *oṃ rī rī hūṃ khaḥ*.

Then, with a mind undistracted and through the excellence of his devotion, during the occasion of worship, he should offer [the substances] to the deities. Because they are the recipients (*saṃpradāna*), the name of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas ending in the dative case is the three-syllable mantra, which is the heart-mantra; this is because of a statement in the *Samāja Tantra*. By the contact of these three syllables, the substances to be presented attain divine color, fragrance, and taste.
For it is stated in the *Catuḥpīṭha*: "When properly offered to the recipient, they reach their perfection. One should give after having consecrated them with these [syllables].

Specifically, among the substances to be offered, such as flowers and so forth, the word *vajra* is used with the seventh case ending (*saptamī*). And there, the word *svāhā* is likewise employed as a suffix. This is for the purpose of indicating the purity of the reality-meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*, due to the non-perception of the gift, the giver, and the recipient. By this, merit is produced that bestows the fruit of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), and worldly fruits are merely exhausted [in the end].
Thus, the meaning of the word *vajra* is explained in the *Paramādya*:
"It is firm, essential, without cavities, and characterized by being uncuttable and indivisible."
Neither burning nor perishing, emptiness is called the vajra.

Thus, the seventh case is for the purpose of indicating the offering of those flowers and so forth when they have been presented. In this context, the word *svāhā* is for the purpose of indicating: "I offer this to you. This rule of mantra is indeed necessary for the sake of worship. According to the statements in the *Hevajra-tantra* and other tantras: "Oṃ āḥ vajrapuṣpa hūṃ svāhā" and "Oṃ āḥ vajradhūpe hūṃ svāhā," one should present the flowers and other offerings emanated from the syllable *hūṃ*.

And thus is the sequence for stringing the mantra: *oṃ āḥ samyaksaṃbuddhāya vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā*. With this, one should offer a flower three times in the center. Here, the seed-mantra of the Perfectly Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) consists of these very three syllables and no other. For the others, however, it should be stated according to their respective requirements. In that regard: in the east, *oṃ āḥ oṃ hrīḥ āryāvalokiteśvarāya vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā*; in the south, *oṃ āḥ maiṃ āryamaitreyāya vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā*.

In the west: Oṃ āḥ gaḥ, to the noble Gaganagañja, vajra-flower hūṃ svāhā. In the north: Oṃ āḥ saṃ, to the noble Samantabhadra, vajra-flower hūṃ svāhā. In the southeast: Oṃ āḥ, to the noble Vajrapāṇi, vajra-flower hūṃ svāhā. In the southwest: Oṃ āḥ hūṃ, to the noble Mañjughoṣa, vajra-flower hūṃ svāhā. In the northwest: Oṃ āḥ, to the noble Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, vajra-flower hūṃ svāhā. In the northeast: [Oṃ āḥ...]
Oṃ āḥ kṣīṃ āryakṣitigarbhāya vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā. One should worship with vajra flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth.
There, one should recite the verses on the Three Refuges and so forth:
Homage to the Buddha, the Teacher; homage to the Dharma, the Protector;
homage to the great Saṅgha—homage always to these three as well.
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds;
I rejoice in the merit of the world; I direct my mind toward the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly;
I generate this mind of awakening for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others.
I generate the supreme mind of enlightenment and invite all sentient beings;
I shall practice the desired, sublime conduct of enlightenment so that I may become a Buddha for the benefit of the world.
I confess all my misdeeds, rejoice in all merits,
and having observed the fast, I shall practice the noble eightfold poṣadha.
For indeed, there is no one in this world who possesses such mental power, nor in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa, nor in heaven, nor on earth— nowhere at all.
Neither in the celestial realm nor in the divine abodes, nor in the cardinal or intermediate directions—
wander throughout the entire prosperous earth with its mountains and forests, for where could there be another man of great renown equal to this bull among men?

[The practitioner], having recited the single verse beginning with "O Mother, one equal to you... (*tvattulyo*), should pay homage. Likewise, having recited all four verses, he should pay homage. In this regard, these are the four verses:
"I pay homage to all the Buddhas, the Victors, who are without rival."
And the physical remains of all those illustrious, perfectly awakened Buddhas.
Where the perfectly awakened Buddhas are born, where they touch enlightenment,
where they turn the auspicious wheel, and where they pass into final nirvana, free from outflows.
I bow down to those places where the Tathāgatas stood, walked, and sat,
as well as where their lion-reclining couches were prepared.
Above, across, and below, in the cardinal and intermediate directions—
to all stupas, whether containing a body or not— I prostrate myself.
In the northeastern direction stands the Best of Bipeds, the Jina named Duḥprasabha; by him these verses were spoken.
Those who praise the Tathāgatas with these four verses do not go to an evil rebirth for thousands of millions of eons.
Do they not go by thousands?
[These are] the four verses.

He who, having himself awakened to Buddhahood— which is without beginning, middle, or end, and is peaceful— has taught the secure and eternal path that is free from fear, for the sake of awakening those who are unawakened.
Homage to him who wields the supreme sword and vajra of wisdom and compassion, the sole cutter of the sprout of suffering,
and the shatterer of the wall of radiance concealed by the grasping of various views.
I constantly bow to the Buddha, whose hand holds the excellent lotus;
who is the very essence of loving-kindness, Gaganagañja, and Samantabhadra;
the lord of yakṣas, Mañjughoṣa, who is ever-striving for the welfare of others.
I bow with devotion to Viṣkambhin and Kṣititanu.
Then, in that regard, one should recite eight times the Queen of Vidyās, who performs offerings of false worship:
"Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! O you who possess the power of the super-knowledges and are honored everywhere, homage be to you, svāhā!"

At the time of making offerings to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, or at any other time, one should recite this hundred-syllable king of mantras, which possesses great merit and is the heart-essence of all Tathāgatas, empowered by all the Buddhas. In this regard, the mantra is as follows:

Homage to the Tathāgatas of the three times, who possess the power of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) that is everywhere unimpeded. Oṃ! Unequaled, equal, you whose teaching brings about the attainment of infinite states on all sides; remove, remove! Remember, remember! O Buddha-nature free from passion! Move! O you who are unequally immovable! Laugh, laugh! Be ashamed, be ashamed! O great covering of the sky! In an instant, blaze, blaze in the ocean, svāhā! Oṃ! To the mass of spreading clouds of offerings, radiate coolness, filling the sky, hūṃ! Having consecrated the offerings with this [mantra] and having expanded them, [one should proceed].
"Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! In every way, O you who have risen (*udgata*), radiate, *maṃ*, throughout the expanse of space in all directions, *svāhā*!

With this mantra of unfailing nature, one should perform worship toward those worthy of honor. Thereafter, through the power of the Buddha’s empowerment and by the force of the mantra-vidyā, [the rite is accomplished].
In the assembly of the Perfectly Enlightened One, born from my own vow.
"May clouds of offerings proceed, established in universal auspiciousness,"—
having thus reflected with effort and with a perfectly steady mind.

Thus: "Then I, named so-and-so, at all times and in every way, offer myself to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with their retinues who have entered the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). May those Great Compassionate Ones empower me, protect me, and grant me the supreme accomplishment in their presence. I confess all sins born of passion, hatred, and delusion, committed throughout all time. One should perform the rejoicing in merit and the dedication of merit according to the previously mentioned verse beginning with, "By those productions of the thought of awakening through which it was confessed... [32r] Thus.
"The welfare of all sentient beings has been accomplished for you, and success has been granted according to your needs.
Go to the realm of the Buddhas, and return once more! Oṃ vajra muḥ svāhā"—with these words, he should dismiss them.
Then,

having consecrated sandalwood and other substances seven times with the mantra "Namo ratnatrayāya namaḥ | Sarvabuddhabodhisattvān Kurukulle svāhā," one should apply a tilaka for the sake of the good fortune of all people.

Although the fruit of making offerings to the Buddha has indeed been explained in detail within the Sūtras, Abhidharma, and Vinaya, nevertheless, drawing from the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāra-sūtra*, it shall be shown here by way of a mere indication.

Mañjuśrī, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to give food of six flavors and divine garments every day to as many pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in all world-systems, and were to do so for as many eons as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges rivers; and if another son of good family or daughter of good family were to see [an image of the Buddha] made of painting or made of a book—this latter person generates incalculably more merit than the former.
How much more so for one who would join their palms in reverence, or offer flowers, or incense, or a lamp? This very person generates incalculably greater merit than that.
And in the *Śrīsamāja*, it is said:
"One should always worship the Buddhas with the five qualities of sensory pleasure according to the ritual."
"By means of the fivefold offerings of worship, one shall swiftly attain Buddhahood"—
this is the ritual procedure for the worship of the Buddha.
For here, there is no fixed rule as to whether the recitation of the desired True Dharma (*saddharma*) should precede the worship of the Buddha or follow it;

therefore, having maintained pure conduct, it may be recited at other times as well. Alternatively, following the sequence of the first and last watches of the night, or specifically during a similar occasion, one should master it by heart and recite it. Herein, only a mere indication of the True Dharma is shown.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Noble Perfection of Wisdom! It is as follows: Oṃ, you who possess the dharma of excellent wealth, the dharma of gathering, the dharma of favoring, the dharma of liberation, the dharma of constant favoring, the dharma of Vaiśravaṇa, the dharma of transformation, the dharma of accomplishing all tasks, the dharma of conforming to equanimity, svāhā!
Oṃ, to Prajñā, the Great Dharma, the intellect that conquers doubt through the Śruti and Smṛti, to the Sustainer, svāhā!

"Oṃ prajñāvardhani svāhā. When this is committed to memory, it yields the same merit as one who has committed a hundred thousand [verses] to memory. Now, one might object: "Is this not mere exaggeration? But this should not be said; for even for women, children, fools, and those of distracted minds—indeed, even for the learned—this dhāraṇī has been empowered by innumerable Tathāgatas as a means for accomplishing the accumulation of merit. It is like a pillar of the Garuḍa-king which acts as an antidote to poison, yet not by virtue of imparting knowledge through the recitation of a hundred thousand [verses]. Thus it should be understood in other cases as well.

Oṃ, homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! Oṃ kile 2! O you who have arisen from the Tathāgatas, O peaceful one, bestower of boons, become the most supreme of the supreme Tathāgatas! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! When this is held upon the throat, it yields the fruit of reciting the *Gaṇḍavyūha-sūtra*.

Oṃ, homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! Oṃ dhunna 2 hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! This is the fruit of reciting the *Samādhirāja-sūtra*. Oṃ, homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! This is the fruit of reciting the *Mahāpratisarā*.
In this manner, the *Triskandhadeśanā-praṇidhāna* and so forth should also be recited; however, they are not written here for fear of excessive detail.
Having constructed the maṇḍala according to the stated sequence, one should likewise worship other desired deities in this very same order.
Now, in this context concerning the undertaking [of vows], the ritual for the bali offering is described because it must necessarily be performed.

Homage to the Tathāgata Surūpa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One. It is as follows: Oṃ suru 2 prasuru 2 tara 2 bhara 2 sambhara 2 smara 2 santarpa [ya 2] svāhā to all the pretas. When this is offered to the Tathāgatas, there arises boundless joy from consuming that bali. For the pretas and for the donor, there is great fruit. And thus are the benefits.

With each single grain, a meal of one *droṇa* of rice is offered to all the *preta*s. One does not become wretched, nor does one become poor. Furthermore, in birth after birth, one becomes very powerful, handsome, beautiful to behold, possessed of great wealth, affluent, long-lived, and free from illness. Having passed away, one is reborn in Sukhāvatī and swiftly attains unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
This is the *surūpā-bali*.
Then:

Homage to the Buddha, homage to the Dharma, homage to the Saṃgha. Namely: Oṃ aṭṭe caṭṭe ṇaṭṭe kuṇaṭṭe khaṇaṭṭe ṭakke ṭhakke ṭarakke urumati rurumati turu hili mili sarvaṅgaṃ dupadaṅgaṃ. Homage to all the perfectly awakened ones! May my mantra-words be successful; may they bring about fulfillment.

Having consecrated [the offering] seven times with mantras and having presented it as a *bali* offering to the Bodhisattvas, one should give it to the various *preta*s at a place supported by pillars. The benefit is as follows: they are liberated from the obscurations of many lifetimes; thereafter, those *preta*s cease to dwell there. They pacify all the misdeeds of the donor and provide protection. They regard him as their teacher (*guru*) without interruption and employ every means [to assist him].

Then, having consecrated a mere portion of food with water three times by means of the three-syllable mantra: *Oṃ inda yama jalaja kha bhūda vahni vāyu rakha cānda sūja māda vāpa tala pātāle aṭhasāpa svāhā |* *Eat this offering (bali)! Smell it! Take the flowers, the meat, and the blood! Accomplish all my purposes! Khānti khuṇi pheṅa gāda!* *The syllable Oṃ is the mouth of all phenomena, because they are unarisen from the beginning.* *Oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.*
The mantra for the bali offering to all beings.

Then, seeing that the vessel containing water was placed at the base of the door and filled by streams of nectar issuing from the five fingers of his outstretched right hand, he recited: "Homage to all Buddhas, O you who look upon all Tathāgatas! Oṃ bhara 2 sambhara 2 hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!"

Having recited this seven times and offered it to the Bodhisattvas, by means of a Magadhan *droṇa* of rice-grains from that alms-bowl, food for distribution is produced. With those [grains], which have become food completely filled with nectar, one should satisfy the hosts of *preta*s by snapping the fingers three times.
The ritual procedure for the *bali* offering of a bodhisattva:
this and other such daily duties should be performed three times a day by one capable of carrying them out.
The Blessed One has also taught the *śrāddha* for those dwelling in the householder stage of life; its procedure is now described.

Regarding the daily *śrāddha*, just as the *śrāddha* was performed by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, while practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva in former times, so do I perform it: *Oṃ, today, on the [specific] lunar day of this month, to my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, belonging to such-and-such lineage, bearing such-and-such names, together with their wives, and to guests—upon these diamond-rice grains mixed with clarified butter and other offerings: ĀḤ HŪṂ SVĀHĀ.* Having recited this three times, one should offer it.
"Just as those Buddhas dedicated [the merit] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, so do I dedicate it"—thus one should dedicate it. By this, may this merit become a cause for liberation.

This same procedure applies to both the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* and the *aparapakṣa-śrāddha*. However, in the case of the *ekoddiṣṭa-śrāddha*, the specific distinction is that one must mention the name and lineage of the person for whom the rite is performed; the rest is as before.

If one wishes to perform it in this manner, then even that which was mentioned regarding the opening of the channels (*nādī*) and so forth, as well as the specific placement of the knees, hands, and face, and the taking up of sesame seeds, *kuśa* grass, and other items—these minor details are themselves worthy of worship; such is the ritual procedure for the *śrāddha*.

Thus, one who performs white (wholesome) actions should realize: "I am impermanent; I am seized by disease and old age; I do not belong to anyone, nor does anyone—mother, father, son, wife, or the like—belong to me. At the time of death, I must depart, leaving everything behind. By means of this realization, a state of constant heedfulness is established. Furthermore, in this way, the manifold evil committed for the sake of what is pleasant or unpleasant [is brought to an end].
It was not known that one must depart after abandoning these things in such a manner.
Having reflected in this way, one should constantly cultivate loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings.
Whatever livelihood is appropriate for each individual, that one should acquire through pure means of subsistence.

One should contemplate [wealth] as being like medicine for the purpose of pacifying hunger, thirst, and so forth. At the end of this passage, there is also a teaching in the *Ugradattaparipṛcchā-sūtra*: "In this regard, householder, a householder bodhisattva seeks wealth through righteous means, not through unrighteous means; he seeks it with integrity, not without integrity; his livelihood is right, not wrong," and so on in detail.
Having thus performed the daily duties, one should partake of food and so forth at the appropriate time.
At the meal, one should first offer a portion of the food as a bali-oblation;
then, one should give it to the *putrahārī* (the child-stealing spirit) and the rest to those who consume discarded food.
In this context, the offering for all beings (sārvabhautika) and the food offering (naivedya) should be presented:
"Homage to all Tathāgatas together with their retinues, who fulfill all hopes; by every means, take me, hāṃ svāhā!"
With this [mantra], one should offer [the gift] to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
With "Oṃ hārītyai kṣīṃ svāhā," one should offer two balls of food to the yakṣiṇī Hārītī together with her sons.
Oṃ, svāhā to those who eat the foremost portion of the rice-ball offering!
To all those who eat the first morsel of food, [I offer] the gift of the first morsel: homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! Oṃ balandade tejomālini svāhā!

Having consecrated the food prepared in the bowl seven times with either *oṃ āḥ hūṃ* or *oṃ āḥ vajrāmṛte hūṃ*, one should drink a mouthful of water—referred to by the term *āpatyāna*. Then, having touched [the lips] with the thumb and ring finger, one should eat five morsels.
Thereafter, one may eat as much as desired.
One should not eat with the mouth full, nor making noise, nor with the mouth wide open; food should be beneficial, measured, and eaten neither too slowly nor too hurriedly.

At the conclusion of the meal: with the mantra *oṃ utsṛṣṭe piṇḍāśibhyaḥ svāhā*, one should give [the food] to whoever eats discarded morsels (*utsṛṣṭapiṇḍāśin*). One should discard the remainder without any expectation of reward.
Immediately thereafter, for the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*):

Having become pure, one should wish for the welfare of all sentient beings. Bestowing the fruit of the gift upon the donors, one should encourage them toward giving food and other necessities themselves, and perform the purification of the food received. By means of reciting the verse: "In this way, may the king, the donor, and all other multitudes of beings always attain happiness, along with the perfection of long life and health."
Through generosity, beings are brought under one's influence; through generosity, even enmities come to an end.
Even a stranger attains the status of a kinsman through giving; therefore, they proclaim generosity to be the foremost.
Generosity is an ornament in this world; generosity is the warding off of miserable rebirths.
Generosity is the staircase to heaven; generosity is auspicious and brings about peace.
Those enjoyments of the bodhisattvas which are inexhaustible and like the sky—
for the attainment of such enjoyments, this gift prospers.

Then, at the time of sleep, having meditated upon the visualized deity and recited the mantra, one should lie down after paying homage to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others by reciting even a single verse.
In this manner, upon rising from bed, one should perform the same during the latter part of the night.
Thus, for as long as one lives, one should perform this daily every day with unbroken commitment; this is the procedure for undertaking the daily duties.
Thus, at the time of hearing the true Dharma, he explains the ritual for the maṇḍala of the Guru, either for the purpose of worshipping the Guru or for the purpose of making a perpetual commitment.

Having constructed the maṇḍala according to the previously described sequence, one should worship it by visualizing Mount Sumeru, the eight continents and sub-continents, and the eight jewels in the center of that maṇḍala. There, in the center: *oṃ haḥ sumerave namaḥ*. To the east: *oṃ yaṃ pūrvavidehāya namaḥ*. To the south: *oṃ raṃ jambudvīpāya namaḥ*. To the west: *oṃ laṃ aparagodānīyāya namaḥ*. To the north: *oṃ vaṃ uttarakurave namaḥ*. To the south of Pūrvavideha: *oṃ yaḥ dehāya namaḥ*.

To the left: Oṃ yaḥ, homage to Videha. To the south of Jambūdvīpa: Oṃ raḥ, homage to Cara; to the left: Oṃ cā, homage to Cāmara. To the south of Aparagodānīya: Oṃ laḥ, homage to Śāṭha; to the left: Oṃ laḥ, homage to Uttaramantrin. To the south of Uttarakuru: Oṃ vaḥ, homage to Kuru; to the left: Oṃ vaḥ, homage to Kaurava. In the center of the Sumeru islands, upon the ground: to the east, Oṃ yaḥ, homage to Gajaratna.

In the south: *Oṃ raḥ*, homage to the jewel of the wife (*strīratna*). In the west: *Oṃ laḥ*, homage to the jewel of the horse (*aśvaratna*). In the north: *Oṃ vaṃ*, homage to the jewel of the man (*puruṣaratna*). In the southeast: *Oṃ yā*, homage to the jewel of the sword (*khaḍgaratna*). In the southwest: *Oṃ rā*, homage to the jewel of the wheel (*cakraratna*). In the northwest: *Oṃ lā*, homage to the jewel of the gem (*maṇiratna*). In the northeast: *Oṃ vā*, homage to the treasures of jewels (*maṇinidhāna*). Then, with devotion, I offer this complete maṇḍala of jewels.

Having recited, "To the gurus, the bodhisattvas, for the sake of attaining omniscience by the world," one should offer [the gift]. When it is given with a resolute intention (*āśaya*), the fruit belongs to the one who has actually given it.
It is proclaimed that the Buddha is the guru, the Dharma is the guru, and the Saṅgha is the guru.
For it is because the Tathāgatas themselves have declared that the Guru alone is the cause in this matter.
Just as the fruit [obtained] from giving to the perfectly awakened ones is such,
for that very reason, the worship of the guru is praised in the sūtras and tantras.
Furthermore, the Sage declared in the Vinayas, the Sūtras, and the Tantras that when giving to others, the fruit corresponds to the worthiness of the recipient.
And so it has been said by the Lord of Speech: "In the animal wombs, a gift yields a hundredfold; in a sinful man, a thousandfold; and in those rich in virtue, a hundred times a thousandfold."

When one has attained detachment from external desires, a gift given to those established on the path becomes a hundred times ten million; furthermore, it results in the bestowal of immeasurable fruits.
To explain the recipients of gifts, the Tathāgata said this:
"What is given to the Saṅgha is as if given to the Three Jewels; it cannot be otherwise, because they uphold the Buddha's Dharma for its veneration."
"Give to the Saṅgha, Gautamī; when given to the Saṅgha, the fruit is great.
And those who will give even very little in my teaching," so says the *Kāśyapaparipṛcchā*.
For eighty thousand kalpas, possessing great wealth and great fruits,
wherever they are reborn, they always remember their giving;
they always practice giving.

Thus, this profound gift to the Buddha indeed yields great fruit. Having taken kusha grass and sesame seeds, when given to brahmins preceded by the formal words [of dedication], it is a supreme gift; no further restriction is required here.
The seers of reality, speaking without regard for the worthiness of the recipient,
have stated that what is said to be "to be accepted" by those of restricted birth does not cause delusion.
On this point, they have also said:
One should not eat food in the company of one from the family of Bṛhaspati;
nor having eaten according to the Mādhavī mode of life, [should one eat] with those of the families of Mlecchas and the like;
nor should a sage himself accept a morsel of food given by washermen and others.
He who is a worthy recipient for giving to a virtuous vessel is praised as one of noble birth.
If one wishes to visit another monastery, then it should be visited after reciting these two verses:
"Exert yourselves! Go forth! Apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha!
Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut!"
For whoever shall practice vigilantly in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering.
Thus ends the rule for the beginner (*ādikarmika*). *Udānavarga* 4.37–38.
Śubhākaragupta, having conceived compassion for the world, points out the true path;
he is a certain sun among men, steadfast in dispelling the darkness of the doctrines of others.
This composition for beginners was made by Prajñākaragupta, who bestows the happiness of all happy rebirths in both worlds, through the power of his long-standing affection [for them].
... completely conquered ... [end]
